extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, literary critics, and readers studying novel craft
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / critical evaluation of novelistic 'aspects' with emphasis on the prophetic mode and on pattern/rhythm: identifying formal qualities (unity, structure, voice, atmosphere, use of sound) and how they function in major works and authors. Uses examples (Dostoevsky, Melville, Lawrence, Emily Brontë, James, Anatole France, Percy Lubbock) to illustrate criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of prophetic fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction has definite characteristics: it demands humility and the absence of a sense of humour; it 'reaches back' (not necessarily to pity and love); it is spasmodically realistic; it gives the sensation of a song or of sound; its face is towards unity rather than the wandering of fantasy; its confusion is incidental rather than fundamental; the prophet composes from a remoter emotional state and does not reflect or 'hammer away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists these as the hallmarks of the 'prophet' novelist (examples: Dostoevsky, Melville, D. H. Lawrence, Emily Brontë). The prophet manipulates intermittent realism and musical/sonic qualities in the work; readers must accept the humility and suspension of the usual ironic/satirical distance. Beware: prophetic writing may seem preachy or alienating if read by the wrong critical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination of ordinary things (prophetic intermittent realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic novelist can 'let a beam of light' touch ordinary objects made vivid — small foreground things become intensely significant: accurate, patient description of trivial things can be part of prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dostoevsky's accuracy about a trial or a staircase; Melville cataloguing whale products; Lawrence describing a field. The 'intermittent realism' often appears as quiet, detailed foregrounding amid larger prophetic passages and helps produce the work's roughness and later remembered smoothness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roughness of surface and later unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic novels often present a rough surface — dents, grooves, lumps and spikes — that provoke reactions while reading, but after the experience the roughness is forgotten and the work becomes smooth and unified in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This roughness is part of the prophetic method: intermittent realism and vivid foreground detail create friction and eventual sublimation into a larger, memorable whole. Critics should note the tension between surface irregularities and the lasting shape of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonic/song quality (voice as song)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophetic novel often 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound' — the voice may sing or have musical/chanting qualities rather than merely narrate events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with authors who 'talk' rather than 'sing' (Forster's critique of Joyce as 'talk, talk, never song'). Look for passages that operate more by rhythm, cadence, and tonal sweep than by propositional argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity-orientation vs fantasy's multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy faces towards unity: its confusion is incidental, and the work is oriented to some integrating sense; fantasy, by contrast, glances about and treats confusion as fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a novel's apparent digressions or muddles are incidental to an underlying unifying motion (prophecy) or constitutive of an intentionally fragmentary, fantasist approach. Examples used: prophetic works (Dostoevsky, Melville) versus Tristram Shandy or Zuleika Dobson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial remoteness and non-reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic writer composes from a remoter emotional state and does not indulge in reflective philosophizing or incessant deliberate workmanship; he/she 'does not reflect' and 'does not hammer away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a voice that seems to transmit rather than to reason or over-explain; contrast with authors whose philosophical reflection or meticulous craft-work (Joyce in certain instances) undercuts a prophetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and suspension of humour in reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy requires humility from the reader and a suspension of the sense of humour (i.e., not sniggering) so as to receive tragic or exalted material on its own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic or reader must adopt a different set of tools when approaching prophetic work; otherwise its value can disappear. The lecture warns that prophetic demands (like Blake's) will be resisted by many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-symbolizing (symbolism can silence the book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning concrete incidents or objects into fixed symbols (e.g., treating the Delight or the coffin as mere symbols) risks silencing the book and losing its roughness and richness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive restraint is advised: even when symbolic readings are plausible, forcing elements into static symbolic roles can flatten the prophetic 'song' and reduce the work's living ambiguity. Use symbolism cautiously and subordinately to experiential reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception and personification of evil
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong prophetic novel often envisages evil as a profound, sometimes personified force (not merely misconduct or social/sexual vice); villains in prophecy differ from conventional literary villains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the author imagines evil — whether it 'slips over the ocean' or is embodied (e.g., Claggart in Billy Budd, Ahab and Moby Dick). Melville's handling of evil is cited as unusually powerful and non-sordid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of innocence as a moral/structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicting an almost radiant innocence (e.g., Billy Budd) that is destroyed or consumed by evil can be a deliberate prophetic strategy to dramatize moral emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the interplay between 'glowing' goodness and a surrounding malice; the contrast is often engineered to produce moral intensity rather than mere plot causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial absence or presence of conscience as aesthetic condition
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's personal conscience (or lack of it) affects the work's reach: Melville's relative absence of a contracting conscience lets his apprehensions be large and universal rather than nervously confined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the writer's moral self-occupation narrows effect (the 'conscience' of Hawthorne) or whether a broader, less personally anxious stance permits more transcendent harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophet-as-preacher risk (preachiness vs rapt bardic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic novelists often carry a minor aspect of preaching; this can be disconcerting and invite criticism, even while a deeper rapt, bardic voice constitutes their greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the double edge: the author may alternate between a rapt creative voice and an irritatingly moralizing one (D. H. Lawrence). Criticism must separate the valuable esthetic core from transient preachiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using confusion/muddle/chaos to externalize passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate muddying or tempest (muddle, chaos, storm) may be used by a prophetess/prophet to let emotions externalize and to make them function as surrounding forces rather than internal character traits (Emily Brontë example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret structural disarray not automatically as incompetence but as an esthetic choice to manifest passion and atmospheric force (e.g., Wuthering Heights' storms and sound dominate words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern as an esthetic aspect (shape/unity of the book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern is a literary esthetic — the 'shape' of a book (unity, symmetry, hour-glass, grand chain) that causes the reader to perceive the work as a whole; it draws most of its nourishment from the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the novel for large-scale shapes (convergence, symmetry, circularity) that produce a pleasure distinct from mere story or plot curiosity. Examples: Thais (hour-glass), Roman Pictures (grand chain), The Ambassadors (hour-glass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of pattern: hour-glass (symmetry / convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An hour-glass pattern: two chief characters or narrative poles converge at a central scene and then recede, producing mathematical precision and aesthetic pleasure (example: Thais; The Ambassadors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify converging character arcs or events that produce mirrored halves; judge how the central scene/turn accomplishes the pattern and whether it enriches story, plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of pattern: grand chain / circular completion
rubrics_metrics.description: A grand-chain pattern links characters or episodes in a chain that eventually returns to its starting point, completing a social or narrative circle (example: Roman Pictures by Percy Lubbock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether incidents are arranged to hand the reader from one scene/person to the next until a satisfying completion occurs, and whether the pattern fits the author's mood and comic/ironic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of pattern to author's mood and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern must fit the author's mood: the same structural device can succeed or fail depending on whether it is congenial to the book's tonal/atmospheric aims (Lubbock's comic sub-acid charity matches his grand-chain pattern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating form, ask whether structure and tone reinforce one another; a forced pattern that clashes with mood will feel artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern springs mainly from plot and requires planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern is nourished by and springs mainly from the plot; it often requires deliberate planning so that details, minor characters and incidents elaborate the main theme rather than merely decorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how plot mechanics contribute to the overall shape; in some works (Henry James' The Ambassadors) 'everything is planned, everything fits' and minor characters 'work' to elaborate the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern may demand sacrifices (authorial trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who wants pattern to triumph may need to make sacrifices elsewhere (e.g., subordinating incidental richness, making details work strictly for symmetry), and this is a permissible aesthetic choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should note what is sacrificed for pattern — loss of loose digression, narrower character freedom — and evaluate whether the sacrifice produces a greater esthetic return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pattern and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: When beauty is the overall shape of the book it is 'pattern'; when beauty operates instead as recurring motion or cadence within the book (not the whole-book shape), call it 'rhythm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel's esthetic effect is primarily structural (a unifying shape or symmetry) or musical/periodic (recurring motifs, cadences). The lecturer reserves 'pattern' for unity-shape and 'rhythm' for other forms of recurring beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perspective as organizing device for pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a narrator/observer (e.g., Strether in The Ambassadors) as an organizing lens can be a deliberate device to shape pattern: everything in the book is adjusted to that observer's vision so that the pattern emerges through his perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how point of view constrains or arranges material for pattern; consider whether the narrator moves the reader as well as organizing the novel's symmetrical or hour-glass effects.
